---

### `src/proxy.js` — Winner charged their full ceiling

`settlePrice` returned `winner.max` unconditionally. The rules say the winner pays the **lesser** of their own ceiling and `loser.max + increment` (the increment read at the loser's ceiling). Fixed:

```js
// was: return winner.max
// now:
return Math.min(winner.max, loser.max + increment)
```

This explains "proxy bidders charged their full ceiling instead of just enough to beat the underbidder."

---

### `src/softclose.js` + `src/auction.js` — Soft-close not applied to every accepted bid

Three separate sub-issues caused auctions to close on schedule while last-second bids were landing:

**a)** `maybeExtend` accepted a `tookLead` boolean and returned early if `false`. The rules say *every accepted bid* inside the window extends the close, regardless of who wins the contest. Removed the `tookLead` gate from the function.

**b)** In the contest path, `auction.js` passed `winner === challenger` as `tookLead` — so a bid from a challenger the standing ceiling beat never extended the close. Now calls `maybeExtend(this, at)` unconditionally.

**c)** In the self-raise path (standing bidder raising their own ceiling), `maybeExtend` was never called at all. Now it is.

---

### `src/auction.js` — Dead heat: challenger won ties

The contest winner was selected with `challenger.max >= standing.max ? challenger : standing`. The rules say a dead heat **stands with the earlier bid** — the standing bidder wins ties. Fixed:

```js
// was: challenger.max >= standing.max
// now: challenger.max > standing.max
```

This also fixed the outbox: a tied challenger now correctly receives exactly one `outbid` notice rather than silently displacing the standing bidder.

---

## What was wrong vs. `docs/tournament-rules.md`, and the smallest fix

**1. "Paired against someone they already played" (§3)** — `src/pairing.js`
An odd-score-group *shortcut* paired neighbours blindly and floated only the last player, skipping the "no unmet opponent" check entirely. Removed the shortcut so every group uses the documented greedy top-down match (a player takes the highest opponent they haven't met; floats down otherwise; bottom group may rematch).

**2. "Bye lands on the top of the table" (§4)** — `src/bye.js`
`chooseBye` returned `eligible[0]` (highest-ranked of the fewest-byes set) — inverted. Now returns the *lowest*-ranked: `eligible[eligible.length - 1]`.

**3. "Tie-break totals don't match the rules sheet" (§5, §7)** — `src/standings.js` + `src/history.js`
Buchholz wrongly added the bye's own points, and included forfeited games (no game was played). Now a bye and any `forfeit` game contribute nothing. To know which games were forfeited, `recordResult` now stores the `forfeit` flag.

**4. "Table depends on the order results are typed" (§2, §5)** — `src/standings.js`
The sort used a `lastSeq` tie-break ("who got there first"), an order-dependent rule that isn't in the contract. Removed it; rows are now ordered strictly score → Buchholz → rating → id, a pure function of the games on record. Misleading header comment corrected.

**5. Late-entry credit wrong (§6)** — `src/roster.js`
`LATE_ENTRY_POINTS` was `1`; league ruling 2019-4 requires a **half-point** bye. Set to `0.5`. The "drawn-but-unreported round doesn't count" rule (`completedRounds`) was already correct — verified, not changed.

- **Trial combined change was charged.** Added guard so it's free and immediate like other trial changes (§9).

gh emailkit, so there is literally one canonicalisation. Display (`email`) stays untouched everywhere, per §2.

## Two real bugs found beyond the failing tests

Auditing against the spec rather than the tests turned up defects the reproductions didn't cover:

1. **`canonicalize()` returned a bogus key for empty local parts.** `p+@gmail.com` → `pat`... fine, but `.+@gmail.com` came back as `"@gmail.com"` instead of rejecting it. §1 requires a non-empty local part, and step 3 (drop tag) and step 5 (drop dots) can each empty it. Worse, that bare key was *shared* — unrelated people would have collided onto one account. It now returns `null`. Note this respects §3's documented order: `a.b+@gmail.com` drops the tag first, leaving `a.b` → `ab@gmail.com`, which is valid (§3's own `pat+@example.com` example confirms an empty tag is fine).

2. **Billing self-destructed its own index row.** My first cut deleted the previous canonical entry before writing the new one — so re-saving the same identity (or `updateEmail` back to it) silently unregistered the customer. Both `setContact` and `updateEmail` now only unindex the old form when it genuinely differs. I also guarded `index.set(null, …)` / `.get(null)`, which would otherwise have created entries that can never be found or deleted.

Because `canonicalize` can now return null for input that passes `parseAddress`, I added a shared `identityOf()` helper so all five services treat "no identity" identically to "invalid-email" — mutating calls refuse and change nothing, lookups answer `null`/`false`/`[]` — instead of each module re-deciding that edge case.

One judgement call worth flagging: §1 doesn't explicitly say whether an address whose local part is *entirely* a tag is invalid. I read "non-empty local part" as applying after canonicalisation, since the alternative lets strangers share an identity key. If support expects `.+@gmail.com` to be a real account, that's the one line to revisit — it lives solely in `canonicalize()`.

The fix was uniform: delete every local key function and route all identity through `canonicalize()`. Display text stays exactly as typed (§2) and is never consulted for matching.

## Two bugs beyond the failing tests

I wrote a throwaway conformance probe against the spec's corners rather than trusting the suite, since you noted the tests aren't the acceptance criteria. It found real problems the reproductions missed:

- **`parseAddress` accepted inner whitespace.** It trimmed only the outside, so `a b@c.co` passed §1 as valid and got stored as an "address". Now any remaining `\s` after trimming is invalid — mutating calls refuse it, lookups return `null`/`false`/`[]`.
- **`setContact` leaked the replaced address.** Re-setting a customer overwrote `contacts` but orphaned the old index entry, so the retired address kept resolving — violating "nothing may keep answering for an address that was replaced." Both `setContact` and `updateEmail` now release the previous key.

Three of my probe's own assertions were wrong, not the code, and worth flagging because they encode a widespread misconception: **dropping the tag does not drop the dots.** `Dana@Gmail.com` is *not* the same identity as `dana.white@gmail.com` (both fold to different forms), and `lee+@gmail.com` collapses to `lee@gmail.com`, since `pat+@example.com → pat@example.com` proves the trailing `+` is stripped too.

## One doc correction

The README example claimed `lookup('dana.white@gmail.com')` finds the account registered as `Dana.White@Gmail.com` and called it "the same" — true by accident (gmail ignores dots), but the adjacent illustration invited readers to assume `Dana@Gmail.com` would also match, which it doesn't. I rewrote the example to show the folding explicitly. The public surface in `src/index.js` is unchanged, per the conventions.

## What was wrong

**1. Percentage channels came out one step off** (`src/rgb.js`)
A percentage was mapped `(pct/100) * 256`, but §3 defines it as a percentage **of 255**. So `rgb(0%, 75%, 100%)` gave `g=192` instead of the documented `191` — the "step off" from the equivalent integer. Fixed to `* 255` (the misleading "256 steps" comment removed too).

**2. Negative hue landed on the wrong sector** (`src/hsl.js`)
`h = h % 360` — JavaScript's `%` keeps the dividend's sign, so `-120°` stayed `-120`, fell into the first sector branch, and serialised as red (`#ff0000`). §4 says a negative angle wraps the same way (-120° = 240°, blue). Fixed with a positive modulo: `((h % 360) + 360) % 360`.

**3. Four-digit hex disagreed with eight-digit** (`src/hex.js`)
For the short form `#rgba`, the alpha nibble was scaled as `nibble(a)/255` — treating a single digit as if it were already a byte. So `#4fa8` gave alpha `8/255`, while `#44ffaa88` gave `136/255`. §2 says the alpha digit is a nibble like any other: **duplicate it**. Fixed to `expand(a)/255`, matching the long form (`#f808` ≡ `#ff000088`).

**4. Translucent swatches lost a notch of alpha on serialise** (`src/serialise.js`)
`toHex` wrote the alpha byte as `Math.floor(a * 255)`. §6 requires rounding **half up**, so `a=0.5` (`0.5·255 = 127.5`) floored to `0x7f` instead of `0x80`. Fixed to `byte(a * 255)`, where `byte` already rounds half up and clamps — keeping the "translucent keeps both digits even at `ff`" behaviour intact.

Each fix was a single root cause, no behavior beyond the spec changed, and the `roundHalfUp`/clamp machinery already matched §1 and §6 so I left it untouched.

**DCCCC re-imports unnormalised → root cause: `format`**
`src/format.js`'s greedy table listed the hundreds place as only `D`/`C` — it had entries for `XC/XL/IX/IV` but **no `CM`/`CD`**, so 900 was written `DCCCC` and 400 `CCCC`. Added `[900,'CM']` and `[400,'CD']` so the walk is canonically descending. `canonicalize('DCCCC')` → `CM`, `format(400)` → `CD`.

**Strict accepts `IL` → root cause: `validate`'s subtractive rule**
The strict validator only rejected a left-of-larger pair when the left symbol wasn't `I`/`X`/`C`, so `IL`/`IC`/`XD`/`XM` slipped through (and `IIII` too — its repeat cap was `> 4`, allowing runs of four). Replaced the hand-rolled checks with grammars that encode section 2 in one pass: `STRICT_RE` accepts *only* the canonical form; `LENIENT_RE` widens just the repeatable symbols to a four-fold additive over-run, while still rejecting illegal pairs and doubled V/L/D in every mode.

**`4000` came back as `MMMM` → root cause: `range` + default `mode`**
`assertInRange` used `n < 0 || n > 4000` — so `0` and `4000` passed and `2.5`/`NaN` were let through (NaN even returned as a sentinel, violating the "rejection means a throw" rule). Now it requires `Number.isInteger` and `1..3999`. Separately, `parse` defaulted to `mode: 'lenient'` against the spec — the default is now **strict**, and any other mode value throws even for a valid numeral. Bad-character/empty input is rejected before the value walk, so no sentinel ever escapes.
